Kangaroo × Jev: reactive navigation benchmark

PAL Kangaroo (4dof arms) in MuJoCo · PAL loco policy v357 · idealized D435 + YOLO26n-seg · run 20261010-221313

Goal in every course: walk to a red cube that is in view from the start. Every second, perception turns the head-camera frame into a scene description; Jev answers 8 questions about it in one request (is each motion safe, how much does it help); code allows only motions with enough measured room and takes the one Jev scores most useful. Walking is PAL's RL policy. The baseline is a short rule over the same description. No map, no pose.

Reached = within 0.9 m of the cube. Progress = share of the start-to-cube distance covered at best. One episode per course and brain, each in a fresh simulation, 90 s limit.

Findings

  • No falls and no wrong-way walks. In 12 episodes neither brain fell; in the previous design Jev walked off an edge on all 4 raised courses. The fix was structural: geometry and the safety margin in code, a floor plane fitted every frame, and 20 s of memory for edges the camera can no longer see.
  • Neither reached the cube within 90 s. Jev covered more of the way on average (46% vs 33%) and was ahead on 4 of 6 courses, level on one and behind on one; it got furthest on pit (84%, round the hole) and walkway_turn (73%).
  • Both get stuck turning. Turns are 65–90% of all decisions, with up to 27 left/right flips per episode: the veto blocks forward near a wall or an edge, each turn looks best on its own, and nothing records which side was already tried. This is the classic local minimum of purely reactive navigation, not a perception error.
  • Jev and the rule agree on 79–90% of steps. Where they differ, Jev more often keeps walking along an open path that leads roughly towards the cube, which is what its progress score was asked to value.
  • Jev's safety answers follow the measured room only roughly (chart below): median p(safe) 0.38 for walking forward without enough room, 0.85 with room, but it still called 64 of 349 forward steps safe without room. The code veto caught every one, which is why the margin belongs in code. One Jev episode grazed a person on crowded_walkway (0.07 m inside the 0.3 m footprint margin).
  • Cost: one request with 8 questions per decision, about 2,300 input tokens (about $0.0001), 0.24 s mean and 0.28 s p95.

Next step. Give the decision a little commitment: a Noul "is the robot going back and forth without progress?" plus the turn direction it last committed to, and let code keep turning that way until a long free run opens. Then repeat each course several times.

Caveats: one episode per course and brain. The machine was heavily loaded by another project during this run (perception 0.4–2.2 s per frame instead of ~0.13 s), so episodes got 38–87 decisions instead of ~90; motions are capped at 1 s so this changes the pace, not what each decision does. The camera cannot see the floor within ~0.8 m; it is covered by the 20 s memory. Film strips are re-rendered from the logged base pose with the joints at the start posture.

Jev's judgments

What Jev sees and decides

Pipeline: D435 RGB-D on the torso (5 Hz) → YOLO26n-seg + depth geometry + red-colour mask + 20 s memory of edges and obstacles → scene JSON → one Jev request with a Noul (safe?) and a Score (progress, 4 levels) per motion → code: geometric veto (forward needs 0.8 m, turns 0.5 m), Jev veto below p(safe) 0.3, then highest progress → fixed velocity command → PAL's v357 walking policy (50 Hz).
